steps.user_message: Here's my situation for 2023 taxes. I'm married filing jointly, live in San Diego CA. My employer Midwest Health Systems paid me $79,400 (W-2). I also earned $8,900 doing consulting for 3 clients, got $920 interest from Marcus savings account and $195 dividends from E*TRADE. I work from home in a 165 sq ft office; rent is $2,100/month, total space 690 sq ft. I paid $4,800 in student loan interest (Cornerstone, 2016–2019), gave $720 to Northwest Harvest (food bank) have the receipt, and had $780 in work supplies. What's deductible? Standard or itemize? How do I handle the home office? What forms or worksheets?
steps.expected_behavior: Agent should help with tax-related questions based on available information.
steps.agent_response:
Short answer up front
- You should report the $8,900 consulting as self‑employment income on Schedule C and you can deduct the $780 of work supplies on Schedule C.
- Because you’re self‑employed you can also take a home‑office deduction (if the office meets the “exclusive and regular use” test). Using your numbers, the actual method (Form 8829) gives a much bigger deduction than the simplified method.
- Student loan interest is an above‑the‑line deduction (up to $2,500, phased out at high incomes). With your wages + expected self‑employment income your MAGI will be well under the phaseout, so you should be able to claim the $2,500 maximum (you paid $4,800 but deduction capped at $2,500).
- Your $720 charitable cash gift is deductible only if you itemize. With the standard deduction for married filing jointly for 2023 of $27,700, it is very likely better to take the standard deduction unless you have substantial other itemizable deductions (state/local taxes, mortgage interest, big medical expenses, etc.).

Detailed walkthrough and calculations (using the numbers you gave)
1) Business income and business expenses
- Consulting gross receipts: $8,900 → Report on Schedule C.
- Work supplies $780 → Deduct on Schedule C as business expense.
- Home office (165 sq ft out of 690 sq ft = 165/690 = 23.913% of the home)
  - Annual rent = $2,100 × 12 = $25,200.
  - Actual-method home office portion of rent = 25,200 × 23.913% ≈ $6,028.70.
  - Simplified-method deduction = $5 × 165 = $825.

Compare effects on net self-employment income:
- If you use the simplified home‑office: net SE income ≈ 8,900 − 780 − 825 = $7,295.
- If you use actual home‑office (rent portion): net SE income ≈ 8,900 − 780 − 6,028.70 = $2,091.30.

Because the actual-method rent portion (≈ $6,029) is allowable and still leaves a positive net profit, the actual method produces a much larger deduction and therefore is probably better for you.

2) Self‑employment tax and above‑the‑line deduction
- SE tax = 92.35% of net SE income × 15.3%. Rough approximate results:
  - Simplified case (net $7,295): SE tax ≈ $1,030.6; half SE deduction ≈ $515.3.
  - Actual case (net $2,091.30): SE tax ≈ $295.5; half SE deduction ≈ $147.8.
- The half of SE tax is an above‑the‑line deduction on Form 1040 (Schedule 1).

3) Student loan interest
- You paid $4,800 but the federal student loan interest deduction is limited to $2,500 (and then phased out at higher MAGI).
- With the numbers above your MAGI will be well below the MFJ phaseout threshold for 2023, so you should be able to claim the full $2,500 on Schedule 1 (Form 1040). (Keep your Form 1098‑E or loan statements to substantiate the interest paid.)

4) Charitable contribution
- $720 cash charitable gift is deductible only if you itemize (Schedule A). Since the 2023 standard deduction for married filing jointly is $27,700, you will almost certainly take the standard deduction unless you have other large itemizable deductions (mortgage interest, large state/local taxes up to the $10k SALT cap, big medical expenses, etc.).

5) Interest and dividends
- $920 interest + $195 dividends = $1,115 total — report on Form 1040. You only need Schedule B if interest + ordinary dividends exceed $1,500 or if you have special situations.

6) Summary of likely outcome (based on the numbers you gave)
- Use actual home‑office method (Form 8829) because it gives ≈ $6,029 vs $825 for simplified; that substantially lowers taxable income.
- Claim student loan interest deduction up to $2,500 (Schedule 1).
- Deduct $780 supplies on Schedule C.
- Likely take the standard deduction ($27,700) rather than itemizing (only $720 charitable shown).
- File Schedule C (profit/loss from business), Schedule SE (self‑employment tax), Form 8829 (if you use actual method), Schedule 1 for student loan interest and half SE deduction, plus Form 1040. Consider Form 8995 (QBI) — you likely qualify for a small Qualified Business Income (QBI) deduction (20% of qualified business income) — this is reported on Form 8995 or 8995‑A (may reduce taxable income further).

Forms / worksheets you’ll use
- Form 1040 (main return)
- Schedule 1 (adjustments to income) — student loan interest, half of SE tax (reported via Schedule SE)
- Schedule C (profit or loss from business) — report consulting income and business expenses
- Schedule SE (self‑employment tax)
- Form 8829 (Expenses for Business Use of Your Home) — if you choose actual method; otherwise use the simplified amount on Schedule C (line for business use of home)
- Form 8995 or 8995‑A (QBI deduction) — if eligible
- Schedule A (only if you itemize) — charitable gifts, SALT (subject to $10k cap), etc.
- Keep: W‑2, 1099‑NEC (if you got them), 1099‑INT, 1099‑DIV, Form 1098‑E (student loan interest), receipts for charitable donation, receipts for supplies, proof of rent paid, and documentation that the home office space is used exclusively for business.

Questions I have / items you should confirm
- Were the $780 of supplies used for the consulting (self‑employment) work, or are they unreimbursed employee expenses for your W‑2 job? (Only self‑employment expenses are deductible now.)
- Did you receive any 1099‑NEC forms from the consulting clients?
- Any other deductible expenses (large CA state tax paid, mortgage interest, property taxes, unreimbursed medical, unreimbursed business travel, vehicle expenses for the consulting, utilities or renter’s insurance you paid separately)? Those could change whether you itemize or not.
- Does your home office meet the exclusive-and-regular-use test and is it your principal place of business? (If not, home-office deduction is not allowed.)

Practical recommendation
- If your home office qualifies, use the actual method (Form 8829) — it looks to be much more beneficial given your rent.
- Report consulting income and expenses on Schedule C, then compute Schedule SE.
- Take the standard deduction on Schedule A unless you have additional itemizable deductions beyond the $720 charitable gift.
- Keep all receipts and Form 1098‑E to substantiate the loan interest deduction.

If you’d like, I can:
- Run the detailed math for both home‑office methods and show estimated AGI, taxable income, SE tax, and estimated federal tax owed/refund using your exact numbers; or
- Draft a checklist of documents to collect before you file; or
- Help you prepare the Schedule C and Form 8829 inputs.

Which of those would you like me to do next?
